TREFACE. 


IIe  White  Book  was  so  little  known  in  the  year 
1884  that  I  was  assured,  by  those  who  professed  to 
have  examined  it,  that  its  text  was  so  fragmentary  as  to  be  of 
no  account.  Having,  however,  been  taught  to  examine  and 
verify  for  mj-self  I  set  about  getting  an  introduction  to  the 
owner,  which  proved  a  vain  effort  for  some  months.  But  one 
day  I  met  on  a  railway  journey  a  gentleman  who  befriended 
me.  Upon  my  application  Mr.  W.  R.  M.  Wynne  of  Peniarth, 
with  that  characteristic  consideration  and  kindness,  which 
I  have  experienced  at  his  hands  for  a  quarter  of  a  century, 
brought  the  Manuscript  up  to  0.xford.  It  was  deposited 
for  my  use  in  the  Bodleian  Library,*  and  allowed  to  remain 
there  during  the  greater  part  of  the  year  1885.  The 
importance  of  the  White  Bookt  was  patent  after  the 
briefest  examination,  and  the  work  of  transcription  was 
begun  forthwith.  I  may,  therefore,  claim  to  be  the  modern 
discoverer  of  the  extent  and  value  of  the  texts  here  printed 
for  the  first  time.  Moreover,  wherever  the  White  Book 
has  been  quoted,  it  has  been  quoted  in  virtue  of  my  labours, 
though  hitherto  without  acknowIedgment.í 

*I  owe  deep  thanks  to  Mr.  E.  W.  B.  Nicholson,  Bodley's  Librarian,  for  his 
kindness,  during  many  years,  in  accepting  responsibiUty  for  the  care  of  dozens 
of  MSS.  deposited  in  the  Library  for  my  use. 

f  White  Book  in  this  preface  is  used  to  denote  Peniarth  MS.  4  only.  This  is 
bound  in  white  veUum  with  MS.  j,  as  one  volume.  An  early  owner  was  named 
RhySerch  or  Roderick,  hence  Pen.  MSS.  4  &  5  are  known  as  The  Whitf  Book  of 
Roderich.     But  no  inconvenience  wiU  foUow  if  we  drop  the  name  of  Roderíck. 

X  Howeyer  egotistical  this  may  appear  on  the  surface,  it  goes  deeper  and  serves 
historical  truth.  Prior  pubUcation  of  certain  passages  and  commenîs  in  the  Noles 
does  not  mean  that  I  am  the  borrower.     My  transcript  was  extensívely  used  in  1886. 


The  general  reader  may  see  no  great  difFerence  between 
the  yersions  brought  together  in  this  work  and  the  version 
of  the  Red  Book  of  Hergest;  but  a  student  of  grammar 
and  language  Hke  the  late  Professor  Strachan,  of  the  Univer- 
sity  of  Manchester,  found  in  the  White  Book  a  key  to 
unlock  many  treasuries.*  The  comparative  mythologist,  and 
the  students  of  hterature  and  romance  will  also  find  in  its 
columns  matter'worthy  of  their  serious  attention. 

The  text  of  the  White  Book  carries  us  back  six  score 
years  or  more  beyond  the  Red  Book,  and  is  I  beHeve  the 
original  of  the  Hergest  text.  If  we  assume  that  both  manu- 
scripts  were  transcribed  from  the  same  archetype  we  should 
hardly  find  both  scribes  making  the  same  mistakes  in  the 
same  places.  That  this  is  the  case  will  appear  in  the  Notes. 
Moreo\er  it  is  certain  that  the  White  Book  was  in  the 
hands  of  the  Red  Book  scribe  of  Kulhwch  &  Olwen, 
because  he  has  filled  in  a  lacuna,  originally  left  blank,  in  the 
text  of  the  White  Book  at  the  foot  of  column  467  and 
the  top  of  column  468.  The  lines  printed  in  italics  are  in 
the  hand  of  the  scribe  who  wrote  the  earlier  and  the  greater 
part  of  the  Kulhwch  in  the  Red  Book.  It  may  be  asked, 
how  could  this  be  done,  if  the  Red  Book  scribe  was  copying 
the  White  Book?  We  can  only  surmise  that  there  were 
other  copies  of  this  romance,  or  that  the  Red  Book  scribe 
had  better  eyes  to  decipher  the  archetype.t  Instances  of 
one  man  reading  what  another  man  declares  to  be  illegible 
are  not  unknown.  Most  eỳes  at  the  age  of  forty-two  can 
read  what  may  appear  blurred,  or  unreadable  at    fifty-five.

Hearty  thanks  for  your  Uindness  in  putting  your  texts  at  my  disposal.  At  present

viii 


That  is  no  uncommon  experience.  The  wise  man,  therefore, 
will  not  attempt  to  edit  difficult  manuscripts  after  his  fiftieth 
year,  not  unless  he  enlists  a  younger  pair  of  eyes  to  do  the 
work,  while  he  confines  his  own  energies  to  the  title  page. 

The  yarious  texts  forming  this  book  were  copied  in  the 
years  1885,  1888,  1893,  revised  twice*  with  the  originals  before 
being  set  up  in  type,  thrice  in  proof,  and  finally  after  the 
text  had  been  electrotyped,  but  before  the  plates  were  used 
for  printing  off  in  1904-06.  Whatever  mistakes  may  be 
left  are,  therefore,  not  due  to  want  of  care.  Wherever  I  was 
in  doubt  I  looked  at  the  originals  over  and  over  again, 
besides  questioning  Professors  Rhys  and  Morris  Jones,  to 
whom  I  gave  off-prints  as  the  pages  were  revised,  and 
now  desire  to  give  thanks,  without  incriminating  either  as 
partakers  of  my  errors.t 

The  method  followed  is  that  of  reproducing  the  manu- 
script  in  all  its  details :  character  for  character,  word  for 
word,  space  for  space,  line  for  line,  column  for  column,  and 
page  for  page.î  This  applies  to  the  whole  book  with  these 
exceptions :  in  the  Gereint  from  Peniarth  manuscript  6, 
part  iv.,  the  page  for  page  has  been  abandoned  in  order  to 
make  the  subject-matter  on  the  opposite  pages  run  con- 
currently.  For  a  similar  reason  both  page  for  page  and  line 
for  line  could  not  be  followed  in  the  case  of  Maxen 
Wledig  from  Peniarth  manuscript  16.  The  same  departure 
at  the  beginning  of  the  second  version  of  the  Peredur  text, 
from  Peniarth  MS.  14,  has  no  better  excuse  than  Iove  of 
symmetry  in  the  printed  page.§

of  Maxen  and  of  Peredur  from  Peniarth  MSS.  i6,  14  &  7 :  and  I  have  to  lhank  hini 
for  the  deletion  of  two  stops  and  the  letter  a  in  yarllaeth,  p.  286'i.

To  indicate  the  present  condítíon  of  the  wrítíng  in  the 
original  manuscripts  here  reproduced,  a  graphic  system  has 
been  devised  by  the  editor.  Letters,  or  parts  of  letters, 
which  are  faint,  and  are  therefore  Hable  to  be  misread,  have 
fìne  dots  placed  under  them ;  those  which  cannot  be  read, 
either  from  the  surface  of  the  vellum  having  been  rubbed, 
torn,  or  cut  away,  have  a  straight  line  placed  under  them  ; 
and  those  whicb  have  been  retraced  by  some  later  pen,  in  a 
way  to  make  the  original  writing  illegible,  are  indicated  by 
a  wavy  underline.  This  method  of  visualising  the  exact 
state  of  the  originals  dispenses  with  a  volume  of  Notes, 
which  otherwise  would  have  been  necessary.  It  also  saves 
the  time  of  every  student  who  uses  the  book  seriously.  He 
sees  at  a  glance  what  readings  are  liable  to  be  mistaken  and, 
if  the  meaning  be  out  of  harmony  with  the  context,  knows 
the  work  of  emendation  should  be  attempted. 

Wherever  leaves  are  missing  from  the  White  Book  the 
text  of  the  Red  Book  has  been  printed.  The  numbers  of 
the  latter's  columns  are  enclosed  within  square  brackets  [  ]. 
The  marginal  numbers  on  pages  97-100  denote  the  hypo- 
thetical  columnar  numbers  of  the  lost  White  Book  text, 
The  Red  Book  text  of  BreuSwyd  Rhonabwy,  by  being 
thrown  into  bi-columnar  form,  occupies  precisely  the  number 
of  the  sequential  folios  missing  at  this  place  in  the  White 
Book.  This  fact  practically  proves  that  the  White  Book 
contained  this  curious  story,  though  I  know  of  no  other 
evidence.  If  we  look  further  and  note  how,  at  the  beginning 
of  Jarlles  y  IFynnon,  this  bi-columnar  arrangement  brings 
us  exactly  to  where  the  White  Book  text  resumes  the 
story  at  page  113,  we  shall  need  no  further  demonstration. 
Pages  II 7- 118,  and  123-124  respectively  represent  folios 
CCxxix  &  CCxxxii  of  the  White  Book.  These  two  folios, 
like   many  others,   have  been   torn  out,  but  unlike  others  a 


fragment  of  each  remains  behind,  containing  that  part  of  the 
text  which  is  underhned.*  By  changing  the  order  of  the 
wordsf  in  the  Red  Book  its  text  dovetails  into  these  frag- 
mentary  hnes.î  We  thus  know  that  the  íwo  texts  must  have 
been  closely  related,  probably  as  original  and  copy. 

The  fragments  of  the  Mabinogion  on  pages  279-282 
are,  in  point  of  writing,  the  oldest  in  this  work,  dating  from 
about  1235.  They  are  specially  interesting  because  they 
prove  that  the  earher  the  text  the  purer  and  more  intelhgible 
it  is  :  they  also  ihustrate  Welsh  prose  at  its  best,  and  rouse 
speculation  as  to  the  date  of  origin.  Unfortunately  examples 
of  the  youth  of  Welsh  prose  are  practically  unhnown. 
Except  for  the  description  of  the  boundaries  in  the  charters 
in  the  Book  of  ILan  Dâv,  and  sundry  other  short  paragraphs, 
nothinghas  survived  earlier  than  the  Black  Book  of  Chirk, 
where  the  style  is  primitive  in  comparison  with  the  above 
fragments  of  the  Mabinogion,  though  the  age  of  their 
respective  manuscripts  is  removed  by  a  generation  only. 
But  the  date  of  a  manuscript  is  no  index  to  the  time  of 
composition,  except  that  no  composition  can  be  later  than  the 
earliest  manuscript  in  which  it  occurs.  Internal  evidence  is 
more  helpful.  Though  we  cannot  compare  narrative  with  the 
technical  parts  of  legislative  prose,  yet  the  Chirk  codex 
contains  sufîicient  examples  of  ordinar)'  prose  to  institute  a 
comparison,  and  it  exhibits  a  syntax  which  is  singularly  pure  : 
it  is  simple  and  direct  in  expression,  and  illustrates  an  earlier 
stage  in  the  growth  of  Welsh  prose  than  the  fragments.  Now 
if  we  examine  the  expanded  versions  of  the  'Yenedotian' 
Code  \ve  fìnd  that  they  exemplify  a  later  stage  than  these 
fragments  of  the  Pedeir  Kainc.     Much,  therefore,  depends

the  case  of  the  Welsh  of  the  aforesaid  boundaries  and  Laws, 
the  original  compositions  are  reputed  to  be  centuries  older 
than  their  respective  manuscripts.  In  as  much  as  scribes,  in 
the  act  of  copying,  modernised,  altered,  edited  their  originals, 
we  are  left  to'build  largely  on  deductions  drawn  from 
their  blunders.  For  instance  Welsh  orthography  for  centuries 
moved  steadily  along  well-defined  Hnes,  every  school  and 
generation  foUowing  recognised  rules.*  This  fact  furnishes 
helpful  guidance,  because  now  and  again  every  scribe 
tripped  by  unconsciously  reproducing  the  spelHng  of  his 
exemplar.  It  is  precisely  these  survivals  of  an  older

got  reduced  to  ef,  înstead  of  cu  ef.  The  first  mistake  could

belonging  to  the  -ou  stage  of  Welsh  ortiiography.*  The

precluding  tlie  possibility  of  its  being  a  century  or  more 
earlier.  The  Four  Branches  of  the  Mabinogi  are,  therefore, 
demonstrably  a  century  older  than  any  manuscript  con- 
taining  them  which  has  come  down  to  our  time. 

The  White  Book  wrítíng  is  in  the  prevailing  style  of 
Süuth-Welsh  manuscripts  of  the  last  quarter  of  the  thirteenth 
century.  The  larger  hand  of  the  early  folios  belongs  to  the 
same  school  as  a  law  manuscript  of  about  1282,  but  the 
White  Book  is  slightly  more  archaic  in  style.  The  several 
hands  are  illustrated  by  facsimiles  found  in  the  second  part 
of  this  book.  They  bear  a  common  family  likeness,  and 
were  probably  written  at  Strata  Florida,  except  the 
Peredur,  which,  as  will  appear  in  the  Epilogue  and  Notes, 
was  probably  written  at  Neath  Abbey,  the  nursery  of  the 
Book  of  Taliessin,  which  belongs  to  an  allied  type  of 
writing,  though  somewhat  earlier  in  date.  The  Gereint 
from  Peniarth  manuscript  6,  part  iv.,  is  in  the  same  hand 
as  the  Taliessin. 

of  Lleu-Sar.  The  dar  clothes  the  anwaeret  to  this  day,  and  helps  to  make  the 
valley  of  the  Llyvni  between  Lleuar  vach  and  Craig  y  Dinas,  one  of  the  most 
picturesquely  beautiful  and  impressive  in  Wales.  Dín-lleu  and  Nant-Ueu  are  well-

The  manuscript  order  of  the  Tales  and  Romances  is 
followed  in  this  work,  but  this  order  is  no  guide  to  the  age, 
or  importance  of  the  compositions,  or  the  last  might  claim 
to  be  first.  The  Winning  of  Olwen  is  the  oldest  in 
language,  in  matter,  in  simplicity  of  narrative,  in  primitive 
atmosphere.  It  has  the  appearance  of  an  assemblage  of 
the  Notes  of  a  professional  entertainer  who  told,  rather  than 
recited  finished.  tales.  In  the  telHng  he  probably  branched 
off  in  many  directions,  clothed  the  dry  bones  of  the  list 
of  names  with  life  and  adventure,  and  touched  on  many 
subjects  but  dimly  understood  to-day.  Some  of  the  oldest 
poetry  reflects  a  similar  world  of  thought  and  action,  and 
both  are  far  removed  from  our  mediaeval  and  modern  liter- 
ature.  The  glamour  of  the  early  morning  dew  is  upon  them, 
when  as  yet  it  was  fresh  and  heavy. 

To  place  the  Kulhwch  thus,  before  the  Pedeir  Kainc 
y  Mabinogi,  is  to  fly  in  the  face  of  authority  and  traditional 
orthodoxy  in  such  matters,  because  it  is  commonly  assumed 
that  nothing  containing  the  name  of  Arthur  can  be  earlier 
than  Geoffrey  of  Monmouth,  as  if  he  had  not  only  changed 
a  national  into  an  international  hero,  but  had  resuscitated 
Arthur  about  1135.  The  name  of  Arthur,  it  is  argued, 
does  not  occur  in  the  Four  Branches,  therefore  they  are  older 
than  Geoffrey.  The  name  of  Arthur  does  occur  in  the 
Kulhwch,  therefore  it  is  later  than  Geoffrey,  or  at  least 
Arthurian  incidents  have  been  grafted  on  older  tales.  It  is  a 
worlíable  theory ;  it  is  clear,  concise,  and  plausible.  But 
for  all  that  the  linguistic  test  of  the  respective  texts  of 
the  White  Book  challenges  it.  Moreover,  the  Four 
Branches  of  the  Mabinogi  are  finished  wholes,  whereas 
the  Kulhwch  is  episodic,  fragmentary.  Its  Arthur,  too,  is 
an  earlier  and  a  more  majestic  type  than  the  Arthur  of  the 
Romances.     He  is  more  of  the  great  leader,   more  of  the 


giiiding  power  behind  the  scenes.  He  has  nothing  about 
him  of  the  later  knight-errant  who  seeks  quarrels,  and 
engages  in  trivial  affairs.  Nothing  is  more  marked  in  the 
Romances  than  the  gradual  degradation  of  Arthur.  The 
later  the  composition  the  more  ordinary  grows  the  great 
leader,  till  at  last  he  is  overshadowed  by  his  leading  knights, 
a  fact  which  makes  it  far  more  reasonable  to  believe  that 
Geoffrey  pillaged  Keltic  Romance,  and  gave  it  a  Norman 
atmosphere,  th.m  the  contrary.  The  idea  that  he  wrote 
ever)-thing  "out  of  his  own  head "  is  childish  ;  while  the 
argument  built  on  the  absence  of  Welsh  manuscripts  before 
his  time  ís  wholly  futile,  because  a  perfected  literature  is 
not  born  in  a  day.  \Ve  have  already  seen  that  the 
Four  Branches  cannot  be  later  than  the  time  of  Geoffrey, 
and  literature  can  show  few  things  more  mature  in  style,  or 
more  full  of  old-world  charm.  They  mirror  a  past  that 
touched  life  with  magic,  with  illusion  and  fantasy.  The 
mythological  and  the  actual,  gods  and  men,  are  so  blended 
as  to  be  undistinguishable,  and  yet  most  natural  in  their 
movements  and  actions. 

Historia  Peredur  ranks  third  in  order  of  age.  It  is 
distinctly  older  than  Gereint  and  Owein  in  language,  more 
W'elsh  in  feeling  and  atmosphere,  and  less  influenced  by 
the  prevailing  tone  of  the  Romances  of  chivalry.  To  the 
student  of  origins  it  is  full  of  problems,  problems  which 
baffle  solution.  One  thing  only  seems  clear.  The  story  is 
old,  and  there  must  have  been  repeated  redactions  of  it  before 
the  days  of  Chretien.  Every  redaction  dropped  some  old 
matter  to  introduce  something  fresh,  or  gave  a  new  turn  to 
old  incidents  in  order  to  meet  the  changed  spirit  of  a  new 
time.  The  later  was  ever  thus  overlaying  and  supplanting 
tlie  older,  and  bringing  about  those  divergencies  in  agree- 
ments  which  characterise   all   versions   known  to  us.      How 


many  redactions  there  were  before  the  last  quarter  of  the 
twelfth  century  we  do  not  know,  and  the  immediate  source 
of  Chretien  is  a  debated  question.  It  might  be  argued  that 
there  was  a  Kymric  historia,  which  was  a  source,  if  not  the 
source  of  Chretien  and  his  immediate  successors ;  that 
Chretien's  fosterhng  was  brought  to  Wales  and  succeeded 
too  well  in  stamping  its  own  image  upon  the  native  story, 
though  it  did  not  efface  all  its  features.  Hence  the  contra- 
dictions  in  the  character  of  Peredur,  who  was  evidently  a 
pagan  before  he  had  been  transformed  into  a  Grail  hero. 
That  he  was  early  known  as  such  in  Wales  is  not  a  mere 
surmise  of  the  writer.  Witness  the  striking  evidence  of  the 
Black  Book  of  Carmarthen  : 

Bet  Mor,  maurhidic  diessic  unben, 
post  kinhen  kinteic, 
Mab  Peredur penweíic.     657-9. 
This  epithet  of  pen-metic  reveals  as  by  flashlight  the  place 
and    character    of   Peredur   in  the    Welsh    tradition    of  the 
twelfth  century ;    he  is  pen-veìsig,  i.e.  the  chief  physician  who 
healed    the    Grail    King.      Thus    an    independent  source  of 
genuine  antiquity  reveals   Peredur  to  us  as  the  Welsh  hero 
of  the  Grail  quest,   the   high  healer  of  the   Gwr  gwynn  cloff 
of  columns  127-130  of  our  text. 

In  so  far  as  the  main  incidents  of  our  historia  correspond 
with  those  of  Chretien  and  Wolfram,  they  are  in  thorough 
accord  with  the  FenveSig  record.  Peredur's  behaviour  towards 
the  damsels  that  fall  in  his  way  is  throughout  consistent  and 
chaste.  He  rights  their  wrongs,  restores  to  them  their  lost 
possessions  from  motiv'es  of  unselfish  compassion,  motives 
unalloyed  by  desire,  and  the  usual  knightly  guerdon  of  a 
maiden's  favour.  He  seeks  neither  leman  nor  wife.  Many 
make  love  to  him,  but  he  presses  ever  onward  in  pursuit  of 
his  quest,  which  brooks  neither  dalliance  nor  delay.  Chretien 
and  Wolfram  neither  comprehend  nor  .sympathise  with  his 
x\i 


celibate*  behaviour.  Their  great  heroes  are  great  lovers,  and 
as  they  found  Peredur  an  unamorous  knight,  they  made  him 
very  like  a  fool.t  Public  opinion  is  on  their  side.  In 
every  age  the  man  who  acts  from  purer  motives,  or  follows  a 
more  self-denying  standard  than  his  neighbours,  is  ever 
thought  to  be  beside  himself,  a  fit  subject  for  jest  and  ridicule. 
Any  way  the  difference  between  the  early  characterisation  of 
Peredur,  and  of  his  French  and  German  aliases,  is  funda- 
mental.  He  is  childlike,  is  pure  in  mind  and  body ;  Perceval 
and  Parzival  are  childish,  half-witted,  clownish.  But  the 
stupidity  ends  as  soon  as  Chretien  and  Wolfram  have 
perverted  their  hero's  conduct  to  square  with  their  ideal  of 
a  knight.  Traces  of  these  perversions  meet  us  latterly  in 
our  text  in  Peredur's  declarations  of  his  love,  and  in  the 
severity  of  his  reveries.  Nevertheless  there  is  nowhere  any 
mention  of  amour  or  wedlock.  The  usual  phrases  for  both 
are  absent,  though  he  is  said  to  have  shared  with  the  Empress 
the  rule  of  her  kingdom  for  fourteen  years. 

It  might  be  argued  further,  that  the  lost  primitive 
version  contained  such  passages  as  those  relating  to  the 
Witches  of  Gloucester ;  and  that  the  survival  of  such  a  frag- 
ment  in  the  Welsh  text  is  presumptive  evidence  of  this.     It

certainly  appears  that  the  initiation  and  training  which  Peredur

forn:i  of  the  historia.  When  Peredur  presents  himself  before 
Arthur,  he  is  sans  all  the  trappings  and  training  of  a  knight. 
The  meeting  with  the  WiSon  must  therefore  come  after  his 
visit  to  Arthur's  court,  but  before  any  of  the  adventures, 
except  the  one  with  bow  and  arrow.  Whether  this  was  with 
some  haughty  lînight,  as  in  the  later  versions,  or  with  the 
Wi(5on  herself  does  not  appear.  All  we  are  told  is  that  the 
Wifon  meets  him  when  he  is  a  raw,  untrained  youth ;  and 
that  she  kindly  takes  him  under  her  tuition  and  protection.* 
She  informs  him  of  his  "  destiny  to  receive  horse  and  arms  " 
at  her  hands,  and  takes  him  home  with  her  "to  practise 
horsemanship  and  to  get  used  to  the  feeling  of  armour  about 
him"  (139-140).  He  therefore  makes  a  three  weeks'  stay 
at  Witchery  Court  before  he  takes  his  departure,  properly 
trained,  and  fuUy  equipped  as  a  knight.  We  are  now 
prepared  for  the  distinction  of  his  subsequent  history,  which 
thus  begins  at  the  beginning,  in  a  simple  old-fashioned  way. 
First  comes  the  country  home  under  the  care  of  the  anxious 
mother ;  as  the  lad  grows  up  his  body  is  exercised  in  roaming 
through  the  forest ;  his  eye  and  mind  are  trained  in  the 
observation  of  natural  objects ;  his  hands  and  arms  in 
manipulating  bow  and  arrows.  Peredur  is  provided  with  fuU 
scope  to  indulge  in  boyish  sport,  and  grows  up  healthy  and 
vigorous.  In  short,  he  has  the  surroundings  ot  the  modern 
ideal  of  boy  life.  With  young  manhood  comes  the  restless 
feeling  which  seeks  adventure  in  the  outer  world.  At  this 
season  Peredur  sees,  for  the  íìrst  time,  knights  in  armour. 
The  sight  fascinates  him,  just  as  the  sight  of  a  well-niounted

words  of  advice,  he  mounts  an  ungroomed  bony  horse,  and

rustic  manners,  the  absence  of  all  conventionality,  and  you 
have  a  spectacle  that  is  sure  to  attract  attention,  and  to  raise 
the  jeers  of  Arthur's  courtly  throng.  The  unexpected  and 
the  unusual  always  cause  laughter,  and  bring  abuse  from 
the  crowd.  Precisely  the  same  thing  would  happen  to-day, 
if  a  high-spirited  youth,  from  some  mountain-home,  pre- 
sented  himself  before  the  King,  in  the  presence  of  his 
Guards,  demanding  a  place  among  them.  There  would  be 
titters  and  trouble.  The  official  Kay,  while  dismissing  the 
uncouth  recruit  to  the  drill  serjeant,  the  riding  school,  and 
the  tailor,  would  be  bound  to  say  something  which  would 
burn  into  his  very  soul.  This  was  the  lot  of  Peredur. 
Conscious  of  his  purpose  and  his  strength,  and  being  rudely 
reminded  of  his  awkwardness  he  quitted  Arthur's  court  in 
wrath,  and  set  out  to  battle  for  himself  with  his  bow  and 
arrows.  Long  practice  had  given  him  unerring  skill  in  the 
use  of  these.  VVe  accept,  therefore,  the  result  of  the  first 
encounter,  though  unforeseen,  as  the  most  natural  thing  in 
the  world.  But  who  can  accept  what  follows  ì  That 
Peredur  should  ride  and  thrust  as  sUilfulIy  in  his  first  as  in 
his  last  tourney  revolts  all  sense  of  art  and  experiencet. 
Something  therefore  has  gone  wrong.  Chretien  has  bungled 
his  source,  or  we  should  not  have  marvels  without  the 
necessary   machinery.     The  expIanation    seems   to  be  this :

Without  the  initiation  at  Witchery  Court  his  unmatched  skill 
and  long  catalogue  of  victorious  encounters  would  be  in-

invincible.  His  early  proficiency  in  arms,  and  the  display  of 
his  skill  before  the  Kaer  y  êol  uncle  become  thus  intelligible. 
Nothing  was  left  for  his  uncle  to  teach,  except  a  few  maxims

childlike  habit  of  quoting  his  mother,  and  of  asking  questions. 
Peredur  then  takes  his  departure.  Nextt  day  he  comes 
to  a  lake  on  which  are  men  fishing  from  a  dug-out. 
On  the  further  margin  is  an  old  man,  whom  he  notices 
to  be  lame  as  he  retires  to  his  castle  close  by.  He  follows 
after,  and  finds  him  seated  on  a  long  cushion :  the  old 
man,  his  uncle,  invites  Peredur  to  be  seated  beside  him. 
While  they  talk  together  he  witnesses  the  memorable 
wonders  of  the  bleeding  lance  and  head.  Mindful  of  his 
recent  lesson  he  forbears  to  ask  a  single  question,  and  thus 
precipitates  the  crisis  of  his  fate.  The  lessons  of  the  firstt 
uncle  were  necessary  and  good,  but  no  advice  is  of  universal 
application.  Hence  followed  quite  naturally  the  story-teller's 
calculated  mistalte.  Without  the  advice  there  would  have 
been  no  mistimed  reticence,  and  without  the  reticence  there 
could  have  been  no  high  quest,  no  devotion  to  an  unselfish 
end,  no  fulfilment  of  destiny,  an,d  no  Historia. 

The  sequence  of  the  foregoing  events,  sketched  from  the 
Welsh  text,  follow  one  another  in  a  natural  inevitable  way. 
By  departing  from  some  such  earlier  version  of  the  historia, 
Chretien  and  his  followers  went  astray.  Their  narrative  is 
inartistic,  because  it  is  ever  at  war  with  the  probable,  and  it

has  no  unity  of  purpose.  Having  cut  the  thread  of  their

From  the  story  of  the  Wiáon,  which  carries  us  back 
to  a  time  when  witchcraft  was  a  power  for  good  no  less  than 
a  power  for  evil,  let  us  turn  to  the  Wiíon  herself.  She  looks 
like  a  Welsh  counterpart  of  the  Greek  Hecate,  who  acted 
contradictory  parts.  Among  her  good  gifts  were  wealth, 
good  luck,  victor)'.  Persons  of  rank  placed  her  image  before 
their  houses,  because  she  was  the  bestower  of  good  and  the 
averter  of  evil.  She  taught  sorcery  and  witchcraft :  all  the

she  was  no  less  cruel  than  kind.  The  Wi(5on  is  similarly  a 
beneficent  and  maleficent  power.  Her  opposite  epithets  of 
gorwen  and  gorhu  shews  this  clearly,  notwithstanding  the 
bungle  of  distributing  them  between  mother  and  daughter. 
The  care  taken  by  her  of  Peredur  at  the  outset  proves  the 
beneficent,  gorwen,  side  of  her  character.  Just  as  Hecate  was 
wont  to  bestow  prosperity  on  youth,  so  the  Wiíon  likewise 
sent  Peredur  forth  a  full-panoplied  prosperous  knight.

to  the  sight  of  arms  by  accident  or  stratagem  ;  both  immed-

The  casting  of  Gwern  "  into  the  burning,"  by  his  mater- 
nal  uncle,  is  also  reminiscent  of  the  way  Thetis  concealed 
Achilles  by  night  in  fire  to  destroy  the  mortal  parts  he  had

Bendigeitvran,  as  Peredur  is  of  the  Gwr  gwyn  cloff. 

With  these  parallels  I  must  stop.  The  question  of  origins 
is  too  complicated  to  be  compassed  within  the  Hmits  of  a 
general  introduction,  and  properly  falls  within  the  province  of 
the  comparative  mythologist.  I  have  picked  up  a  few  stones 
fûund  on  the  track,  and  tried  to  register  the  direction  of  the 
purely  Welsh  evidence,  as  seen  through  one  pair  of  spectacles, 
regardless  of  theories  or  consequences.*  Even  a  master 
of  the  whole  field  of  evidence  in  many  languages  would 
think  it  folly  to  dogmatise,  because  dogmatic  statements  are 
the  squinting  children  of  the  special  pleader,  who  mistakeshis 
own  limitations  for  the  frontiers  of  truth.  The  research  student 
will,  therefore,  wisely  keep  an  open  mind  on  this  and  every 
subject,  and  bear  in  mind  that  all  stories  and  all  ideas  are  the 
products  of  evoIutionary  growths  and  fresh  combinations.  No 
version  of  Peredur  is  original  in  the  sense  of  being  the  first 
story  of  the  kind.  Internal  evidence  points  to  three  maint 
stages:  I.  a  pagan  story,  having  traits  in  common  with  the 
Greek  AchiIIes  &  the  Irish  Fionn  ;  2.  a  grail  story  grafted 
on  the  pagan,  in  which  the  Wi8on  played  a  preternatural 
part ;  and  3.  the  survived  versions,  which  are  an  amalgam  of 
Norman-French  chivalry,  Grail  quest,  and  paganism.  As  no 
Welsh  student  can  hope  to  understand  many  things  in  the 
Peredur  without  reading  Wolfram  and  Chretien,  he  would  be 
well-advised  to  read  Miss  Jessie  Weston's  translation  of 
Wolfram   von  Eschenbach's  Parzival,  if  he  cannot  read  the 

*  Nothing  is  more  dangerous  to  inquiry  than  an  altempt  to  bring  discoveries  into 
conformity  with  some  system  or  theory.  It  leads  to  undue  emphasis  being  laid  on 
what  supports,  and  undue  neglect  of  what  saps  such  theory  or  system. 

tThe  first  and  second  may  have  undergone  repeated  revisions,  and  changes. 


original  in  the  excellent  edition  of  Ernest  Martin.  The  French 
version  is  practically  inaccessible,  but  soon  it  is  to  be  hoped 
that  the  text  of  Chretien  and  his  continuators,  in  MS.  12,576 
of  the  Bibliothèque  Nationale,  will  be  made  available. 

The  next,  in  the  order  of  subject,  are  the  Romances  of 
Owein  and  Gereint.  These  reflect  a  different  world,  a  world 
where  the  purpose  and  object  of  life  are  changed.  The 
machinery  is  thè  machinery  of  chivalry,  but  the  whole  atmos- 
phere  is  comparatively  modern.  Love,  marriage,  and  jealousy 
are  the  themes,  and  tournaments  the  method  of  promoting 
them.  Hence  they  are  denominated  chwedyleu  in  the  Welsh 
text ;  they  are  '  stories,'  not  '  history '  like  the  Peredur.  The 
medieval  Welsh  scribes  were  conscious  of  a  difference  oî  genre 
between  these  two  romances  and  the  Peredur,  and  they  were 
right.  The  outlook  is  changed.  The  ideal  has  given  way  to 
the  real ;  the  spiritual  to  the  actual ;  love  to  matrimony ;  un- 
selfish  devotion  to  personal  ends.  Welsh  literature  draws  its 
best  inspiration  from  magic  and  its  spells,  not  from  arms  and 
combats.  There  is  much  of  native  colouring  in  Owein 
and  Gereint,  but  the  fact  cannot  be  blinked  that  both  have 
been  influenced  by  Norman-French  Romances  to  a  greater 
extent  than  the  Peredur.  The  true  relations  of  the  Welsh 
and  French  versions  will  appear  when  the  passages  parallel 
in  them  are  placed  side  by  side,  and  published  by  the  lady 
student  who  has  already  done  much  of  the  work.  Both 
Romances  assumed  their  present  form  in  the  first  half  of  the 
thirteenth  century.  The  oldest  MS.  of  Gereint  emanates  from 
Neath  Abbey,  or  its  neighbourhood. 

The  Adventure  of  Lluá  and  Llevelys  appears,  first  of 
all,  in  the  earliest  Welsh  translations  of  Geoffrey's  Brut,  and 
cannot  be  earlier  than  1200  in  its  Welsh  form.  The  Dream 
of  Maxen  also  belongs  to  the  same  period.  Both  have  been 
happily  characterised  as  Romantic  British  Historj'. 


As  a  composition  there  can  be  no  doubt  that  the  Dream  of 
Rhonabwy  is  the  latest  in  this  work.  The  turn  of  phrase  and 
the  Yocabulary  are  startlingly  famiHar  to  the  modern  man.  The 
characters  are  mostly  well  known  in  the  older  literature  of 
Wales,  and  the  introduction  of  these  lends  an  ancient  air  to  the 
story.  But  to  place  it  earher  than  the  second  half  of  the  thir- 
teenth  century  would,  in  the  opinion  of  the  writer,  be  a  mistake. 
In  the  foregoing  remarks  there  has  been  neither  an  attempt 
to  analyse  the  subject-matter,  nor  to  compare  it  with  kindred 
lore  in  other  iiteratures.  That  far  pleasanter  and  more  exciting 
work  may  be  attempted  later.*  It  commands  a  greater 
and  a  more  grateful  public  than  work  which  demands 
scrupulous  adherence  to  fact,  and  denies  to  fancy  the  unfolding 
of  her  wings.  By  the  most  scrupulous  adherence  to  the 
authority  of  the  manuscripts,  in  matters  great  and  small,  the 
present  texts  aim  at  being  permanent  contributions  to  the 
literature  of  their  subject.  It  is,  therefore,  not  desirable  to 
associate  with  them  discussions  of  problems,  which  every 
generation  will  view  differently,  and  which  none  will  soIve  to 
the  satisfaction  of  the  next,  nor  even  to  its  own.  This  must 
continue  so  long  as  important  manuscripts  remain  unedited, 
and  necessarj'  Iinks  in  the  chain  of  evidence  are  lost  to  view. 
It  seems  to  be  a  rule  with  Time  to  reveal  its  past  imperfectly. 
It  is  shy  or  cryptic  about  this,  allusive  about  that,  while  it 
skips  a  third  altogether  as  a  thing  not  to  be  mentioned, 
whether  from  modesty,  shame,  or  indifference  we  never  know. 
We  are  left  to  unearth  what  we  can  where  we  can,  each 
worker  reporting  his  "  find,"  without  always  discovering  its 
true  place  in  the  temple  of  the  past.  The  White  Book,  as 
our  find,   is  presented  as  a  stone  for  the  building,  unchipped 

'This  work  has  already  been  extensively  done,  in  Germany  by  Professors  Zimmer, 
Foersler,  and  Golther;  in  France  by  the  late  M.  Gaston  Paris,  M.  Lot  and 
M.  Meyer  ;  in  England  by  Mr.  Alfred  Nutt,  Sir  John  Rhys,  and  Miss  Jessie  Weston. 
Good  worlc  has  also  been  done  in  Araerica,  and  more  raay  soon  be  expected  from 
that  Continenl. 

XXV 


and  unharmed  by  efforts  to  shape  it  to  fit  a  particular  place. 
What  hammerings  have  been  done  appear  as  Notes  at  the  end 
of  the  volume.  Manifest  scribal  errors  have  been  corrected 
in  these  Notes,  which  also  contain  attempted  elucidations  of 
certain  obecurities  in  word  and  phrase.  These,  all,  the  writer 
offers  to  the  student  as  suggestions.  Solutions,  alas,  are  not 
always  his  to  give. 

The  word  Mabinogion  has  been  used  many  times  as 
a  title  and,  in  virtue  of  the  associations  connected  with  that 
use,  has  acquired  a  meaning  which  embraces  the  contents  of 
the  present  work,  though  correctly  it  has  a  more  restricted 
sense.  Alabinogi  is  a  derivative  of  maban,  which  is  the 
diminutive  of  mab,  a  son  or  youth.  We  find  it  thus  used  as 
the  synonym  of  the  Latin  infantia  in  Peniarth  manuscript  14.* 
This  use  may  be  compared  with  the  Norman  -  French 
E7ifances  as  applied  to  Perceval.  No  evidence  has  been 
produced  in  support  of  the  view  that  "  mabinog  was  a 
"  technical  term  belonging  to  the  bardic  system  and  meaning 
"a  literary  apprentice.  In  other  words  that  mabinog  was  a 
"young  man  who  had  not  acquired  the  art  of  making  verse, 
"but  one  who  received  instruction  from  a  qualified  bard." 
If  we  follow  Peniarth  MS.  14,  and  for  'mabinog'  in  the  last 
sentence  read  'Jesus  Christ,'  the  author  of  thedefinition  must 
shrink  from  his  own  words,  and  all  will  see  how  fanciful  they 
are.  It  would  be  more  correct  to  say  that  any  narrative 
which  treats  of  early  life  is  a  mabinogi,  of  which  the  plural  is 
mabinogion,  a  term  applied  in  this  work  only  to  Pwyll  and 
Branwen,  to  ManawySan  and  Math.  But  it  might  be 
extended,  with  the  strictest  propriety,  to  the  Enfances  of 
Peredur,  to  such  a  hanes  as  that  of  Taliessin,  and  possibly  to 
Kulhwch  and  Olwen. 

*  Pen.  MS.  14  contains  The  Apocryphal  Gospet  of  the  Pseudo-Matlhew.  This 
appears  to  be  a  translation  of  the  same  version  as  the  Latin  text :  De  infantia 
Jesu  Christi  edited  by  Tischendorf,  (edilio  altera). 


The  pagínation  of  the  present  work  is  not  on  orthodox 
lines.  It  is,  therefore,  necessary  to  inform  the  reader  that 
though  gaps  occur  in  the  paging  between  56  and  59,  132  and 
193,  254  and  279,  yet  the  text  is  complete.  Theexplanation 
is  this.  The  White  Book  foUos  were,  in  the  fifteenth  century, 
numbered  in  Roman  letters.  These  fix  its  original  e.xtent, 
and  have  enabled  us  to  deduce  the  contents  of  the  lost  parts.* 
It  was,  therefore  necessary  to  make  the  columnar  numbers 
dependent  on  these.  When  a  blank  leaf  bears  a  folio  number 
iu  the  manuscript,  there  is  nothing  in  the  printed  text,  hence 
there  are  no  columns  numbered  113- 116.  Be  it  observed 
that  the  number  of  any  given  page  is  always  half  the  number 
of  its  second  column  ;t  also  that  wherever  two  texts  face  each 
other  the  pagination  is  in  duplicate,  otherwise  the  paging  of 
the  predominant  partner,  the  White  Book,  would  go  wrong, 
and  so  make  all  expIanation  as  to  its  missing  parts  confusing. 
If  therefore  any  reader  should  imagine  that  his  copy  does 
not  contain  312  pages,  let  him  remember  the  pages  re- 
duplicated  and  the  facsimiles.  What  is  apparently  missing 
in  one  place  is  in  evidence  in  another  part  of  the  book. 

The  columnar  number  has  been  adopted  as  the  unil  of 
referencel  in  the  N  o  t  e  s  and  I  n  d  e  x.  The  columns  run 
1-112,  117-261,  385-507,  605-32,  637-48.  In  the  rest  of 
the  book  the  reference  is  necessarily  to  the  page :  these  are 
marked  by  the  letter/.  For  example  :  '120-2'  means  column 
120,  line  2  ;  but  '  p.  120-2  '  means  page  120,  line  2.  Where  a 
secondary  text  faces  that  of  the  White  Book,  the  reference  is 
to  the  latter  only,  unless  there  be  an  alternative  name,  or 
variant,  requiring  to  be  recorded  in  the  Index. 

Mabinogi  occurs  altogether  five  times — in  Pen.  MSS.  4,  &  14.  Matan  is  found 
in  Aneirin  3-9,  31-22;  and  the  plural  mcíẃ  in  B.B.C.  13-11.  Does  OTaíŵof  occur 
anywhere  in  medi^eyal  literature?  *See  p.  131  col.  2,  and  Notes. 

fThis  does  not  apply  to  the  text  of  MS.  7,  i.e.  cols.  605 — 48. 

X  Reference  to  ẁe  pages  would  be  obviously  confusing  and  complicated,  because 
50  many  are  in  duplicate,  and  most  are  in  double  columns. 

xxvii 


I  have  to  thank  Mr.  Alfred  Nutt  for  reading  a  proof  of 
this  preface,  and  for  giving  me  the  benefit  of  his  criticisms. 
But  this  does  not  imply  agreement  on  his  part  with  what  is 
said.  My  friend,  Mr.  Llywarch  Reynolds,  has  also  read 
these  preliminary  excursions  to  their  advantage,  and  I  owe 
him  special  thanks  for  his  interest  and  sympathy  in  all 
that  pertains  to_  the  history  of  this  book. 

Since  the  foregoing  was  set  up  in  type,  one,  to  whom  I 
owe  nearly  all  my  opportunities  of  working  at  Welsh  manu- 
scripts,  has  gone  to  his  rest.  Of  his  kindness  to  me 
personally  I  cannot  speak  too  warmly,  nor  too  strongly.  For 
five  and  twenty  years,  the  late  Mr.  Wynne,  whenever  I 
frequented  his  home,  treated  and  entertained  me  as  a  friend 
and  honoured  guest.  I  never  knew  him  to  grudge  either 
time  or  trouble  to  help  me  or  any  other  student,  who  went  to 
Peniarth  to  work.  Noblesse  oblige  was  the  rule  of  the  house, 
and  careful  thought  was  given  to  all  who  entered  it.  The 
late  Professor  Strachan,  the  last  student  to  visit  Peniarth,  must 
also  have  felt  this  strongly  for  he  wrote  eight  days  before 
his  death :  "  I  have  never  come  across  more  obliging  or 
more  hospitable  people." 

I  must  also  place  on  record  here  my  grateful  sense  of 
obligation  to  Mrs.  Wynne  for  her  unvarying  thoughtfulness 
in  promoting  my  work  and  welfare,  during  my  many  visits  to 
consult  the  originals  of  this  book.  May  the  dews  of  heaven 
fall  thick  in  blessings  on  the  loneliness  of  the  old  home.

261        R.   B.  of  Hergesf. 


HiRTY  leaves,  namely,  folios 
'(JC,v:.\xvij — CClxvj,  are  missing, 
after  next  page,  in  Penierth  MS.  4. 
Of  these,  folios  CCxxxvij — ccl  are 
seemingly  lost,  and  the  nature  of 
their  contents  is  a  matter  of  con- 
jecture.  Happily  folios  CClj — CClviij, 
which  contain  Historical  and  other 
Triads  as  well  as  some  Poetry,  are 
simply  misplaced  :  they  now  form 
pages  117 — 132  of  Peniarth  MS.  12, 
and  their  text  was  published  in 
Y  Cyininrodor  {ox  1884,  pagesi23 — 
154.  As  regards  the  remaining 
folios  CClix — cc!xvj,  they  were  in 
existence  in  February  1573,  when 
Richard  Langford  fortunately  copied 
them  "  in  a  good  light  where  the 
sun  shone,"  he  having  nevertheless 
to  "  strain  his  eyes,  because  the 
writing  was  both  so  dark  and  old." 
Langford's  transcript  however  has, 
like  its  original,  disappeared,  but 
John  Jones  of  Gelli  Lyvdy  has  left 
us  a  copy  of  it  in  Peniarth  MS.  1 1 1, 
pages  117 — 169,  where  we  are  cate- 
gorically  told  that  Langford's  origi- 
nal  was  part  of  Llyfr  Gwyn 
Rhydderch,  i.e.  Peniarth  MS.  4. 
Moreover  we  know  that  the  existing 
folio  CClviij  ends  with  the  opening 
lines  of  Englynion  Gercint  vab 
Erbin,  and  as  Langford  gives  us 
the  concluding  lines,  it  follows  that 
he  had  folio  CClix.  This  fact  estab- 
üshes  the  identìty  of  the  fragment 
he  copied  as  folios  CCli.x — CClxvj.

507  R.  B.  of  Hergest. 


^^^HE  WlNNING  OF  OLWEN 
^I^/  is  the  last  in  the  sequence  of 
Tales  in  Peniarth  manuscript  4. 
The  rest  of  this  voIume  is  made 
up  üf  fragments  of  the  Mabinogi 
of  Branwen  and  of  Manawydan, 
three  pages  of  Gereint,  and  a 
second  text  of  Peredur,  nearly 
complete.  The  pagination  jumps 
from  254  to  279  because  of  the 
pages  in  duplicate  earlier  in 
the  book.  After  this  note  follow 
the  concluding  lines  of  MS.  6, 
part  iv.,  which  could  not  face 
page  226  without  interrupting 
The  Story  of  Kulhwch  ù^  Olwen.
